rationale:
Phase 4 of the site-delivery build needs two customer-facing HTTP links: /d/<token> to download the finished site's ZIP, and /c/<token> to record that the customer has moved their site (and any bought domain) off our infrastructure. The confirm click IS the state by owner ruling 2026-08-19 (no form, no reply parsing), and it is what stops the weekly chase email.

THE HONEST SHAPE OF THIS SUBMISSION: only /c/ is here. /d/ was specified to 'mint a clamped presign and redirect', and I stopped building it when I found it cannot be done in any standing service without reversing a standing owner directive. MEASURED 2026-08-21: B2_APPLICATION_KEY_ID is unset in the running pods of agent-chassis, auth-service, core-manager and admin-dashboard; the only manifests carrying B2 credentials are adapters, the database-backup CronJob, and spawned-pod templates. The mechanism, not just the measurement: they were REMOVED from the standing agent-chassis on 2026-08-11 under bugs_open/245, whose first line records the owner's words 'the agent chassis shouldn't carry b2 credentials'. Giving core-manager a B2 key would hand a standing service exactly what another standing service had taken away ten days earlier. Five options are costed in DECISION_2026-08-21b_zip_download_link_needs_a_credential_home.md and put to the owner; none is applied.

WHAT IS NEW HERE THAT REVIEWERS SHOULD PRESS ON: this is the FIRST publicly-reachable route on core-manager. There is no Ingress in this cluster at all (kubectl get ingress -A is empty); customer traffic reaches the webdesign.uk box, whose nginx listens on loopback behind a cloudflared tunnel and proxies NAMED PATHS to cluster services over WireGuard. /stripe/webhook -> auth-service is the proven instance of that shape and this is the second. The exposure is exactly the paths nginx names, which is why the nginx location is a bounded /c/ prefix and the comment forbids widening it: core-manager's site-facts relay reasons explicitly about not being publicly fronted, and this must not quietly make that false.

The route is mounted OUTSIDE AuthMiddleware because the token in the path IS the credential: 32 random bytes, stored only as a SHA-256 hash, expiring, single-purpose and scoped to one site. That is the existing platform/delivery contract (migration 511, DGH-014), unchanged by this submission.

A HAZARD I HAVE NOT FIXED AND WANT LOOKED AT: /c/ is a GET that mutates state, which is what an emailed confirmation link must be given the no-form ruling. Mail scanners prefetch links in email. Such a fetch stamps the site as transfer-confirmed with no customer involved, and if the token were minted single-use it would also spend it so the customer's own click then fails. The lockout half is a one-argument fix at the (unbuilt) minting site: mint confirm tokens NOT single-use, since the stamp is already COALESCEd. The false-confirm half needs a second click, which may or may not count as 'a form' under the ruling. Raised to the owner in the decision doc rather than decided here.

plan.summary: Add GET /c/<token> to core-manager: the customer-facing confirm-transfer click. Handler + a small deps seam + one route mounted outside AuthMiddleware + HTTP-layer tests, and the nginx block that will expose it (written, not deployed). No schema change, no change to platform/delivery, and deliberately no /d/.

edits.rationale: The HTTP surface for the confirm click. Returns 200 with HTML on success AND on every failure: the reader is a customer, and a 404 from a link we emailed reads as 'we have lost your site'. All failure reasons render ONE message, which is the same rule delivery.ErrTokenNotFound already encodes at the data layer, carried up to the layer a stranger can actually observe. A database fault renders a DIFFERENT message ('something went wrong at our end') because telling a customer their link is invalid when it is not sends them chasing a problem they cannot fix, at a service that answers no questions.

A one-method seam so the handler's tests exercise HTTP behaviour without a database, while the SQL semantics stay covered where they already are: platform/delivery's own tests, which run against real Postgres in a rolled-back transaction. now() is injected because token expiry is a time boundary and a handler reading the wall clock cannot be tested at one. The site id returned by ConfirmTransfer is deliberately DROPPED: nothing on the page varies by site, and a page that named the site would confirm to whoever holds the link that the token is real and which site it opens.

One route, mounted at the ROOT and OUTSIDE AuthMiddleware, immediately after the site-facts relay so the two unauthenticated routes and their reasons sit together. Root rather than /api/v1 because this path goes in an email to a customer and gets read aloud and retyped. Outside AuthMiddleware because the token IS the credential. The comment states what makes this route different from everything else in the service: it is the first publicly reachable one, and the exposure is exactly the prefix nginx names.

Every case is written so that removing the behaviour it covers makes it FAIL, and each was proved to by mutating the handler and re-running. The fake confirms ANY token by default, which is what makes the oversized-token case a real assertion rather than a vacuous one: delete the length guard and that request reaches the fake, succeeds, and renders the success page. Asserting 'the dependency was not called' would have proven nothing by comparison. The boundary is tested in BOTH directions: a token at exactly maxTokenLen must still succeed, or the guard is off by one and would reject real tokens the day the format changes.

The block that will expose the route, written now so it ships with the change that needs it rather than being reconstructed later by someone reading Go. NOT DEPLOYED by this change: applying it is nginx -t and a reload on the box. A rate limit IS wanted here, unlike on the Stripe path (where throttling would delay payment confirmation): guessing tokens is exactly what a bot does, and no real customer clicks a confirmation link twenty times a minute. Keyed on CF-Connecting-IP per the file's existing warning, because $binary_remote_addr behind this tunnel is one global bucket for every visitor.

plan.risks:
BLAST RADIUS, measured rather than asserted. (1) No behaviour changes for any existing caller: the only edit to an existing file is an added route registration; no handler, middleware or query is modified. go build ./... and go vet on the touched packages are clean, and platform/delivery's own tests still pass unchanged. (2) The route is INERT until two separate things happen that this change does not do: nothing mints a confirm_transfer token anywhere in production (the delivery email is not built), and the nginx block is written but not deployed. So /c/ is reachable only from inside the cluster today, and would answer 'that link is no longer active' to anything that reached it. (3) The new exposure, when nginx is deployed, is exactly the /c/ prefix on core-manager -- NOT core-manager generally. I regard that as the sharpest thing here and would rather a reviewer disagreed with me now than later: core-manager holds every site's data, and the site-facts relay in the same file reasons explicitly about core-manager not being publicly fronted.

WHAT I DID NOT DO, deliberately: no schema change, no change to platform/delivery, and no /d/ route. The download link needs object-store credentials that no standing service holds by owner directive (bugs_open/245, 2026-08-11, 'the agent chassis shouldn't carry b2 credentials'). Five options are costed and put to the owner; a session picking one quietly is the failure mode I am avoiding.

KNOWN HAZARD, NOT FIXED: /c/ is a GET that mutates state, which the no-form ruling requires. Mail scanners prefetch links in email; such a fetch stamps a transfer as confirmed with no customer involved, and if the token were minted single-use it would also spend it so the real click then fails. The lockout half is a one-argument fix at the unbuilt minting site (mint NOT single-use; the stamp is already COALESCEd). The false-confirm half needs a second click. Raised to the owner rather than decided.
